stances.claim: In litigations between parents, the children's interest is paramount — and this principle, not the parents' procedural maneuvering, controls the disposition of custody.

notable_anecdotes: The Dec 8, 2017 MOA in which David paid Harryvette P2.5 million 'in exchange for the joint custody of their children' — a striking monetary-overlay on a custody arrangement that the Court did not let override the children's-interest paramount.
Harryvette's home-CCTV monitoring of her children from France — a vivid example of remote OFW parenting that the Court treated as effective continuing exercise of parental authority.
The Court's blunt characterization of David: 'habitual drinking, smoking, and history of violent behavior' — used as the dispositive comparative-caregiver evidence against the father.
Joselyn Espiritu, the maternal grandmother, designated by notarized document and elevated by the SC to provisional custodian over the children — used as the model of allowable familial delegation.
Leonen's terminology refinement ('primary' instead of 'sole') — endorsed by the author as a doctrinally cleaner phrasing because custody can evolve with circumstances.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban distills the ratio decidendi of David Carnabuci v. Harryvette Rowena Tagaña-Carnabuci (July 22, 2024, Second Division, per J. Jhosep Y. Lopez, recently released unanimously): in litigations between parents, the children's interest is paramount; even while abroad, the mother is preferred over the father in sole custody of children under seven; her OFW work being temporary, she can visit them occasionally (as she did three times); though parents have joint parental authority, the mother may delegate her sole custodial rights provisionally to a caring maternal grandmother, subject to the father's visitation rights on Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays -- and he may bring the children to nearby amusement parks accompanied by their maternal grandma. The facts: as a married couple, David (an Italian entrepreneur doing business in PH) and Harryvette sired two children, then 3 and 2, when David filed a petition for habeas corpus to gain custody from Joselyn Espiritu, the maternal grandmother. In 2017, the couple separated after four years of marriage; a Dec 8, 2017 MOA had David giving Harryvette P2.5 million 'in exchange for the joint custody of their children.' Harryvette later moved to France as an OFW, leaving the children to David's care; when she learned David left them to other people without her consent, she took the children and placed them under Joselyn through a notarized document. The RTC denied David's habeas corpus and awarded exclusive parental authority and permanent custody to the mother, with Joselyn caregiver and David visitation; the CA modified to joint parental authority, sole custody to the mother, and provisional custody to the grandmother; the SC upheld the CA. The Court stressed that the mother should not be considered 'absent' simply because she was an OFW -- being an OFW does not strip parents of their right to exercise parental authority or the wives' sole custody. The mother monitored children via home CCTV, communicated regularly, and provided monthly financial support; though not ideal, the children received attention and care from both mother and grandmother. The 26-page decision found Joselyn a better caregiver than David due to his 'habitual drinking, smoking, and history of violent behavior'; since the children (then 7 and 8) were already accustomed to living with Joselyn, sole custody was awarded to the mother and provisional custody to the grandmother. The Court emphasized that both parents retained joint parental authority -- separation did not automatically revoke it -- and the father was granted visitation rights under specified conditions. In his separate opinion (to which the author concurs), Senior Associate Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen wrote that while he agreed with the decision, he believed the custodial right of mothers should be termed 'primary,' not 'sole,' because 'sole' implies absolute and exclusive custody -- 'which is not the case, because custody can change depending on later circumstances.'
